svg.aria-label: LLMD on ZML. One LLMD engine serves OpenAI-compatible HTTP APIs and runs many models. Each model is written once in Zig from reusable components; Qwen 3.5 is shown as an embedding, a decoder layer of RMSNorm, Gated DeltaNet or attention, RMSNorm and MoE repeated N times, an LM head and sampling. Each operation picks the best kernel per platform, such as DeepGEMM MegaMoE, FlashMLA or FlashAttention, written in the most appropriate DSL. ZML compiles the models and kernels and runs them through the PJRT C API on NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, Trainium, Intel, Apple, Furiosa and CPU.

rect.data-source-detail: The OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint accepts messages and returns a completion. Clients can also stream the generated content.
The embeddings endpoint converts input text into a vector. The model output is pooled on the device.
The Decision endpoint evaluates typed questions against one shared state. Questions can depend on earlier answers.
The slide labels Prometheus as the observability interface.
Applications and agents send HTTP requests to LLMD. Chat clients can receive generated content as a stream.
The Jinja2 engine in Zig formats conversation messages into the prompt expected by the selected chat model.
Tokenizers turn input text into token IDs. The diagram lists BPE, WordPiece and SentencePiece.
The serving engine handles tool calls returned by the model.
The scheduler combines work from active requests into batches. Chunked prefill lets it process a prompt in pieces.
The engine batches prefill and decode work.
The engine stores attention keys and values in pages. Requests with a common prefix can reuse cached state.
A drafter proposes candidate tokens for the target model to verify.
The host prepares the next execution step while the device runs the current one.
LLMD can divide tensors or experts across devices, or distribute inputs across model replicas.
The engine prepares weights in the layout expected by the selected kernel.

svg.text: Each model is written once in Zig

rect.data-source-detail: The embedding stage looks up a vector for each token ID and passes those vectors to the decoder.
The Qwen 3.5 row shows RMSNorm before the sequence operation and again before MoE.
The Qwen 3.5 decoder row shows these as alternative sequence operations between its two RMSNorm blocks.
The Qwen 3.5 row shows RMSNorm before the sequence operation and again before MoE.
The Qwen 3.5 decoder example shows a mixture-of-experts block after its second RMSNorm.
The language model head maps the decoder output to scores over the token vocabulary.
The sampler uses the model’s output scores to select tokens for generation.
The embedding stage looks up a vector for each token ID and passes those vectors to the decoder.
The Qwen 3.5 row shows RMSNorm before the sequence operation and again before MoE.
RoPE appears in the slide’s row of reusable model components.
Attention appears both in the Qwen 3.5 decoder example and among the reusable components.
Gated DeltaNet appears both in the Qwen 3.5 decoder example and among the reusable components.
Sparse MLA appears in the slide’s row of reusable model components.
The Qwen 3.5 decoder example shows a mixture-of-experts block after its second RMSNorm.
The example mixes residual streams before and after the attention and expert computations.

svg.text: The best kernels, in the most appropriate DSL for each platform:
CuTe · CUDA Tile · Triton · FlyDSL · Mosaic · NKI · Metal · TCL
each operation picks the best kernel per platform

rect.data-source-detail: The original connections are labeled “runs programs” and “loads weights.”
Specialized kernels written in these languages can be embedded in the model graph alongside portable operations.
The compiler generates MLIR from Zig model code, with one program per shape bucket. The diagram identifies StableHLO, Shardy (sdy) and func dialects.
Model authors express tensor operations in Zig, including matrix multiplication, gather, scan and sort.
ZML uses the PJRT C API to compile programs, transfer buffers and execute through a platform plugin.
The NVIDIA target uses CUDA. The schematic lists CuTe, CUDA Tile and Triton for custom kernels.
The AMD target uses ROCm. The schematic lists FlyDSL and Triton for custom kernels.
The Google TPU target uses libtpu, with Mosaic for custom kernels.
The AWS Trainium target uses Neuron, with NKI for custom kernels.
The Intel target uses oneAPI, with Triton for custom kernels.
The Apple target uses Metal for the runtime and for custom GPU kernels.
The Furiosa target uses the Furiosa SDK, with TCL for custom kernels.
The schematic includes x86 and Arm CPUs as framework targets.
